trigger_conditions: injection molding equipment present in plant inventory
hydraulic-driven press technology indicated or unresolved
anti_triggers: all-electric press fleet already in service
injection molding not in scope (e.g., assembly-only plant)
press fleet less than 10 years old AND already electric
falsification_conditions: press fleet inventory confirms electric servo presses across all relevant production lines
production hours below threshold where capital replacement economics make sense
hold-phase parasitic load already measured and bounded as immaterial share
evidence_required: press fleet inventory with drive technology (hydraulic / hybrid / electric servo)
press cycle counts and production hours per machine
annual energy intensity baseline (kWh per ton of product or per shift-hour)
capital replacement schedule for press equipment
financial_translation: Hydraulic injection molding carries parasitic pumping losses during hold phase that electric servo presses do not. When production hours are high, the hydraulic-to-electric swap is a capital-grade efficiency lever whose payback depends on cycle counts and electricity price. Conservative framing: lever is plausible but evidence-bounded.
allowed_language: Hydraulic-to-electric injection molding upgrade is a plausible capital-grade efficiency lever requiring press inventory and cycle-count evidence before underwriting.
prohibited_language: this saves X kWh per machine

source_basis.specific_reference: DOE Better Plants 2022 Progress Update, p. 4 — Legrand North & Central America case study: 'replacing aging hydraulic injection molding units with more energy efficient electric units' listed among notable energy-saving projects
